pages.description: Each resource entry carries three sets of codes on its last line: group codes (e.g., AA Asian American, BA Black American, MF Minority Female, H Handicapped), grade-level codes (E elementary, J junior high, H high sch...
pages.title: Three-set coding scheme (group, grade level, subject area) with column-aligned codes and group indexes

pages.description: Check the learner, contrast, intended outcome, instrument and timing before interpreting or comparing a reported effect size.
pages.title: Comparing learning intervention effects

pages.description: Because explicit learning outcomes are often sector-specific, non-standardized, and not aligned with course content or assessments, the article recommends comparing programs through analysis of significant summative a...
pages.title: Compare courses for transfer by analyzing implicit outcomes in summative assessments rather than calendar descriptions

pages.description: The article proposes a data-driven item-deletion procedure: identify candidate items via the k0 intersection acceptance region (k0 ± 2SD of item scores, difficulty or discriminating values), skewness of the parameter...
pages.title: Delete items only when test reliability improves upon deletion

pages.description: Systematically gathering information about learners' prior knowledge, skills, motivations, and constraints to inform instructional design decisions.
pages.title: Learner Analysis

pages.description: Systematic investigation of learners' prior knowledge, characteristics, and the instructional environment before designing instruction, so that design decisions fit who will learn and where.
pages.title: Learner And Context Analysis

pages.description: Learner personas are evidence-based composite profiles of representative learners used to ground design decisions in real audience characteristics.
pages.title: Learner Personas

pages.description: A companion inventory, also emerging from thematic data analysis, classifies learner responses to mediation hierarchically.
pages.title: Reciprocity inventory of learner responsiveness to mediation

pages.description: Task analysis identifies the prerequisite skills a target performance requires by repeatedly asking what a learner must already master, arranging the answers into a sequenced learning hierarchy from foundational to complex.
pages.title: Learning Hierarchy Task Analysis

pages.description: The paper models a strategy of conceptual clarification: rather than abandoning a fertile but empirically elusive construct, link it to a concept with greater behavioral vulnerability.
pages.title: Make ambiguous behavioral-science constructs empirically tractable by linking them to better-behaved concepts from related nomological networks

pages.description: A design method that lays out the chain from a programme's activities and outputs to the outcomes it is meant to produce, so that each link can be examined, and later tested, on its own.
pages.title: Logic Model

pages.description: A design strategy that surfaces and names power dynamics among stakeholders, making decision-making authority explicit and redistributing it across the design process.
pages.title: Make the Invisible Visible (Power Dynamics)

pages.description: The principle of multimediatizing \"consists in the direct expression of a didactized content into a multimedia form\".
pages.title: Multimediatizing: express didactized content directly in multimedia form rather than digitizing pre-edited media

pages.description: A systematic process for identifying the gap between current and desired performance and determining whether instruction is the right remedy.
pages.title: Needs Analysis

pages.description: Hunt recommends sequential ordinal scales, inspired by Piaget's observations, as an alternative to norm-referenced mental-age and IQ metrics.
pages.title: Assess early development with sequential ordinal scales that disentangle development from age

pages.description: Mueller's paper translates Piagetian theory into a fifteen-item yes/no behavioral checklist covering environment organization, heterogeneous grouping, learner decision-making, cooperative interaction, active methods,...
pages.title: Piagetian teacher behavioral congruency checklist for analyzing teaching styles

pages.description: The paper's concluding recommendation is that student-model designers consider replacing a static learning rate with a recency adjustment to Bayesian updates, because this \"can lead to better properties of knowledge e...
pages.title: Apply a recency adjustment to Bayesian knowledge-estimation updates instead of a static learning rate

pages.description: An appendix study applied and modified Hooper's mathematics taxonomy to symbolic representations of heat and temperature in three widely used LAUSD physical science textbooks.
pages.title: Taxonomy of ten symbolic representation types for heat and temperature in high school science textbooks

pages.description: Choosing, adapting or combining an instructional design model for a project. ADDIE is treated as the underlying process and each model as a context-specific instance of it, chosen by delivery format and by what the project must produce.
pages.title: Selecting an Instructional Design Model

pages.description: A design method that enumerates the parties who participate in, govern, fund, or are affected by a learning activity, gives each a stable identity, and records only the relationships that change a design decision.
pages.title: Stakeholder Mapping

pages.description: Deriving a course's goal tree from an external framework — a standards set, competency model or certification blueprint — and carrying the framework's own codes through objectives, activities and assessment items so that coverage and provenance stay traceable in both directions.
pages.title: Standards Crosswalk

pages.description: A systematic method for breaking down a complex skill or task into its component knowledge, skills, and decision points so instruction can be designed around what learners actually need to master.
pages.title: Task Analysis

pages.description: A design method that reasons backward from a desired long-term outcome to the preconditions it requires, making explicit both the links the design controls and the assumptions it depends on but does not.
pages.title: Theory of Change

pages.description: A design recommendation for research synthesis methodology: because bias is inherent in primary research and many synthesist choices are glossed over, the article urges that \"Synthesists need to be rigorously transpar...
pages.title: Synthesists should be rigorously transparent in design, write-up and provision of supplementary materials so others can check, replicate or modify syntheses

pages.description: The article organizes fuzzy forecasting as a reusable two-step procedure.
pages.title: Two-step fuzzy forecasting pattern: fuzzylise the universe, then interpret the fuzzy output

pages.description: The article recommends AMOVA as a post hoc addition to instrument validation practice, claiming it \"adds considerable value to the methods designed to assess instrument validity and reliability especially when said in...
pages.title: Use AMOVA to add validity and reliability assessment value for researcher-designed instruments, with further substantiating research

pages.description: A reusable whole-task policy for complex skills: learning tasks in simple-to-complex task classes with fading support, supportive and just-in-time procedural information, and selective part-task practice, whose response-dependent branches are untested proposals.
pages.title: 4C/ID (Four-Component Instructional Design)

pages.description: A reusable policy for tutoring by software, from step-based intelligent tutoring systems to conversational AI tutors and pedagogical or teachable agents: decide how much the tutor gives away, keep the learner doing the reasoning, judge it on unaided performance rather than assisted practice, and decide when a human tutor or mentor takes over.
pages.title: AI Tutoring

pages.description: A reusable policy for building a lesson or unit around a shared narrative or media scenario: check that solving the anchor's problem requires the target concept, guide novices through it rather than leave them to search, connect the anchor explicitly to the concept, and judge the unit on individual use of the concept in a new situation.
pages.title: Anchored Instruction

pages.description: Assessing a capability through an extended task that mirrors real practice, with public criteria, feedback and revision before the final judgement, is expected to improve performance and transfer of that capability for learners who already have its components; no claim here tests authentic assessment against conventional tests, and guidance for novices, untrained self-assessment and scorer disagreement limit it.
pages.title: Authentic Assessment

pages.description: Diagnosing learners' spontaneous speech, choosing a short list of features across suprasegmentals, segmentals and fluency, teaching each explicitly and then in communicative use is expected to improve listeners' understanding of learners' spontaneous speech; no claim tests the balanced curriculum, and the nearest evidence shows explicit instruction reliably improves controlled production of targeted features, with smaller, less certain gains in spontaneous speech.
pages.title: Balanced pronunciation curriculum covering suprasegmentals, segmentals, and fluency, with a short list of central features selected by diagnosis

pages.description: A reusable course-level policy that assigns each part of a course to online or in-person work by what that mode does that the other does not, with the in-person time spent on practice and interaction and the online part supported for self-regulation and persistence; the wiki holds no test of the blend itself apart from the extra time and materials it usually brings.
pages.title: Blended Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy for learning from realistic cases: establish what learners can already do with the target concept, have them compare several cases that share a principle rather than study one at a time, make the principle explicit, and judge the unit on transfer to a new case rather than on enjoyment or recall.
pages.title: Case-Based Learning

pages.description: A reusable modeling, coaching, scaffolding, fading, articulation and exploration policy for complex cognitive skills, whose phase transitions depend on observed unaided performance and remain an untested design proposal.
pages.title: Cognitive Apprenticeship

pages.description: Learners who judge work against shared criteria alone, compare their judgments in a small group and then with a reference judgment are expected to judge new work more accurately and to improve their own work, where they know the domain well enough to see quality and the ratings carry no grade; no claim tests collaborative evaluation itself, and the evidence is peer-assessment, rubric-training and judgment-accuracy studies carried to it.
pages.title: Collaborative Evaluation

pages.description: A reusable policy for joint work that elicits each member's starting response, chooses a task that needs the members' reasoning, and uses individual checks rather than the group's product or self-report to choose the next activity.
pages.title: Collaborative Learning

pages.description: A reusable course-level policy that maps a course to stated competencies, places each learner by a criterion-referenced response, lets pace vary and advances on demonstrated competence, with the validity of the evidence, the support offered, time and completion stated as conditions.
pages.title: Competency-Based Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy in which learners infer a concept's defining attributes by comparing labelled examples and non-examples, then classify new instances; expected to improve classification of new instances where the concept has identifiable attributes, the examples are chosen to contrast on them, guidance and a stated rule follow the induction, and learners can already interpret the instances.
pages.title: Concept Attainment

pages.description: Constructive alignment is expected to raise performance on the intended capability when the stated outcome, the practised activities and the assessed task demand the same performance at the outcome's level, with practice and feedback before assessment; no claim here tests alignment itself, and one study found practice above the assessed level served a lower-level exam better.
pages.title: Constructive Alignment

pages.description: A reusable policy for small-group work that elicits each member's starting response, sets interdependence and individual accountability together, and uses individual checks rather than the group product to choose the next activity.
pages.title: Cooperative Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy for structured argument on a contested question, in which preparing, defending and answering opposing cases is expected to improve individual argument, conditional on an arguable resolution, evidence and questioning in the rules, moderated turns, a debrief, and an individual outcome at a stated horizon.
pages.title: Debate

pages.description: For a learner meeting a concept or principle, a lesson that elicits their existing ideas, explains the idea while refuting any wrong one, guides its use with self-explanation prompts, checks on a changed item and connects it by comparing cases is expected to improve explanation and prediction on new cases, though no claim tests the sequence as a whole; its components are tested separately.
pages.title: Develop Understanding

pages.description: A reusable explicit-teaching policy for a structured target (elicit, explain and model, guide practice with checks, hand over on unaided success), qualified by task-specific expertise, outcome type and horizon.
pages.title: Direct Instruction

pages.description: A reusable course-level sequencing policy: an epitome of the most general ideas, elaborated level by level toward detail and tied back to the whole by learner-built synthesis; one small study of hierarchical knowledge organisation bears on it, and no claim tests the sequence itself.
pages.title: Elaboration Theory

pages.description: A reusable policy in which the teacher starts from a planned entry point, records what learners show sustained interest in, webs that interest to content worth learning (and to required standards), follows the thread with guided activity, and closes it on a product or shared account; expected to deepen engagement and self-directed inquiry, mainly with young children and with an adult guiding the activity, but no claim in this wiki tests it against a planned curriculum.
pages.title: Emergent Curriculum

pages.description: A reusable policy in which learners take a role in a simulation of a profession's work and learn its way of deciding; expected to improve decisions justified in the practice's terms where the practice has been studied, mentors model decisions and feedback and debriefs are given, and the outcome is judged outside the game; no claim in this wiki tests epistemic games.
pages.title: Epistemic Games

pages.description: A reusable routine in which learners answer, in talk or writing, what they experienced or read, what they think of it, what they learned and what more needs to be known, expected to improve understanding of content where the learned-answer prompt is content-specific and checked and learners can already make sense of the experience; no claim tests the routine as a whole, only parts of it.
pages.title: Experience with Languaging Activities (ELAs) guided by a sequence of experience-based questions

pages.description: A reusable sequence of bounded experience, prompted debrief, a stated and checked principle and a changed attempt with feedback, repeated across sessions with support fading, is expected to improve performance and near transfer where learners can interpret the experience; no claim tests the cycle as a whole, only its steps.
pages.title: Experiential Learning Cycle

pages.description: A reusable elicit–interpret–act–reobserve policy, qualified by what a response can establish and by whether a relevant next action is available.
pages.title: Formative Assessment

pages.description: A reusable research-and-teach cycle in which learners become expert on one part of a shared theme, teach it to peers in jigsaw groups and read through reciprocal teaching, expected to raise each learner's understanding of the whole theme where research is guided, teaching is structured and every member is checked on every part; no claim tests the pattern as a whole, only its components.
pages.title: Fostering Communities of Learning (FCL)

pages.description: A reusable lesson policy that moves a learner from an observed starting response through presentation, guided and independent performance with feedback, to a check at a stated horizon, keeping or dropping each event according to what the learner's responses show rather than running all nine by rote.
pages.title: Gagné's 9 Events of Instruction

pages.description: A reusable policy in which progress through short, cumulative levels depends on passing a check on the target, with attempt-feedback-retry lessons, review of earlier levels and points paid for accuracy and improvement rather than activity; expected to raise performance outside the app for itemisable, practice-heavy skills, but no claim tests the combination as a whole, only a mastery gate without a game layer, a game layer without a gate, and one app's level system on in-app measures.
pages.title: Game-Based Mastery Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy in which learners make a media product for a real audience to learn its content and media skills: study exemplars, learn the content (explicitly, for novices), plan a blueprint checked for content, produce in roles, revise against criteria and present; no claim tests learning by producing itself, and the sequence rests on neighbouring claims about projects, guidance, audiences, teaching others and the quality of learner-made representations.
pages.title: Learning by Producing (multimedia production as learning)

pages.description: A reusable unit policy in which learners first meet a task that makes a concept necessary, build it through guided inquiry with explicit synthesis, then use it in a consequential task and revisit it later; no claim in this wiki tests the model as a whole, and its phases rest on neighbouring claims (problem-first teaching helps conceptual learning and transfer when instruction builds on the attempts, guided inquiry beats unguided discovery for novices).
pages.title: Learning-for-Use (LfU) Model

pages.description: An open course at a scale where no teacher can answer each learner is expected to serve registrants who can direct their own study only if it replaces teacher time with short segments and self-checks, a planning activity and recurring prompts, calibrated peer review and audited automated scoring, and judges itself by each learner's purpose rather than completion over all registrants; no claim tests a MOOC against another course form, and the nearest tested components are an if-then planning activity that raised completion for some online learners and rubric guidance for peer raters.
pages.title: Massive Open Online Course (MOOC)

pages.description: A reusable gate-correct-recheck policy for cumulative units: elicit a criterion-referenced response, interpret a shortfall, give responsive correction and recheck on a parallel task before advancing, with time, attempts and the outcome horizon stated.
pages.title: Mastery Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy for supporting learners in asynchronous, self-paced online courses and programmes through mentors, coaches or instructors who are available on demand and who reach out proactively: what to set up at the start, which progress signals trigger contact, what a contact does, how automated outreach and AI help divide the work with people, and how to check who the support actually reaches.
pages.title: Mentor Support in Self-Paced Online Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy for pairing an explanation's words with an informative picture, choosing placement, channel, pacing and segmentation from the learner's observed response and the intended outcome.
pages.title: Multimedia Learning

pages.description: An online course whose structure stays constant, whose weekly cycle builds interaction with content, the teacher and peers by design, whose first week centres on contact with a person and whose discussion is structured to reach a conclusion is expected to raise end-of-term performance and completion over one left to chance; no claim tests this, and the nearest claims bear on self-regulation support, if-then planning for completion and where online learners drop out.
pages.title: Online Course Design (Community of Inquiry)

pages.description: A reusable policy for teaching an emergent phenomenon (natural selection, collective behavior) by naming five dimensions on which decentralized, collective causation differs from sequential, individual causation and having learners use them while running an agent-based simulation; one quasi-experiment with pre-service teachers tests it, finding a near-transfer advantage over the same simulations without the framing, trends on deep understanding and misconceptions, and no far transfer.
pages.title: PAIR-C Framework (Pattern, Agents, Interactions, Relations, Causality)

pages.description: A reusable question, individual vote, peer discussion, revote and explanation policy for conceptual questions, with an isomorphic individual check to separate revised reasoning from copying.
pages.title: Peer Instruction

pages.description: A reusable session routine in which paired learners who have studied the material take turns preparing and teaching it to a partner who must respond, correct errors with a scripted move, swap roles and are then checked alone; meta-analyses test peer tutoring and teaching against no tutoring or studying, WWC reviews of the scripted PALS routine find early-reading gains and small, often nonsignificant or null effects elsewhere, and no claim tests the doses, role swaps or hand-over points.
pages.title: Peer Teaching

pages.description: For a whole school, teaching three to five positively stated expectations in every setting, acknowledging them specifically, reviewing disaggregated discipline data monthly and adding daily small-group and then function-based individual support for students who do not respond is expected to reduce referrals and exclusions; one group-randomized trial in 37 Maryland elementary schools found fewer office referrals and small gains in teacher-rated behaviour, largest for children at risk at baseline, but no difference in out-of-school suspensions, and one quasi-experiment found fewer suspensions only where all three tiers ran with fidelity.
pages.title: Positive Behavioral Interventions And Supports

pages.description: A reusable policy for rehearsing an interpersonal or professional performance with a simulated person (a standardized or virtual patient, a simulated client, customer or colleague, avatar or simulated students, a pedagogical agent, or an AI role-play partner): name the performance and how it will be judged, give novices an example first, run short repeated encounters with feedback and a debrief after each, vary and harden the scenarios across sessions, and judge the unit on a blinded performance with a different person rather than on in-simulation scores or satisfaction.
pages.title: Practice with Simulated People

pages.description: A reusable policy for problem-centred units: establish what learners already know of the target content, guide novices explicitly, use a problem-first phase only where learners can generate partial solutions and instruction follows, and judge the unit on individual outcomes.
pages.title: Problem-Based Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy for teachers: one observable classroom practice is modelled, rehearsed, enacted with the teacher's own students and given feedback in coaching cycles over a term, with support faded and use checked later; expected to change observed practice where the target is specific and coach time is sustained, though no claim here compares it with one-off workshops.
pages.title: Professional Development

pages.description: A reusable sequence in which content is broken into small frames, each needing an active response that is confirmed or corrected at once, with progress at the learner's pace or by branching on the response, behind a unit check; expected to help with facts, rules and procedures that have checkable answers when steps fit prior knowledge and a dated schedule guards against non-completion. No claim in this wiki tests programmed instruction itself; the nearest evidence is from self-paced mastery programs (PSI), feedback after retrieval and intelligent tutoring.
pages.title: Programmed Instruction

pages.description: A reusable policy in which learners work on an authentic project, pause it at a diagnosed gap in a component skill, practise that skill in a separate instructional space to an explicit criterion and then resume the project; expected to improve individual mastery and transfer where gaps can be diagnosed and instruction delivered, but no claim in this wiki tests the design as a whole.
pages.title: Project Space and Instructional Space

pages.description: A staged policy for handing learners control over goals, resources, pace and evaluation within a structured course, with a written plan, taught self-direction moves, dated check-ins and calibrated self-evaluation; no claim in this wiki tests the hand-over as such, and learner control alone showed a near-zero effect while self-pacing cost completion.
pages.title: Self-Directed Learning

pages.description: A reusable plan–monitor–act policy that makes regulation explicit with task-specific prompts, modelled self-assessment and a usable next action, then reads the response before handing regulation to the learner.
pages.title: Self-Regulated Learning

pages.description: For a group present in an educational decision process but structurally unable to exercise its decisions, giving it a body with written decision standing, meetings redesigned around its language and agenda, facilitation handed over across the cycle and a report-back on every recommendation is expected to sustain its participation and change what is decided where outreach and interpretation alone do not; one before/after case in this wiki tests a version of this, and the rest is participants' accounts.
pages.title: Shared power: previously excluded students, families, and communities co-create and shape educational systems, policies, and practices

pages.description: For school-age learners, a sustained programme, delivered mainly by their own teachers, that explicitly teaches one named social or emotional skill at a time, rehearses it actively with feedback and has the other adults around them (staff, and families of young children) cue it in daily routines and academic work is expected to improve those skills most, and conduct, distress and achievement by smaller amounts, with gains persisting at follow-up; meta-analyses test universal K–12 SEL programmes as a whole against controls, but no claim tests this sequence's steps, adult learners or one-off formats.
pages.title: Social Emotional Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy for distributing learning opportunities, preserving total practice, gap and assessment horizon when comparing schedules.
pages.title: Spaced Learning

pages.description: A reusable policy for cooperative argument on a contested question, in which pairs argue assigned positions, restate and then reverse them, and write a joint conclusion, expected to support each learner's reasoned, individually checked position, conditional on an arguable question, evidence for both sides, an individual check and a stated horizon; untested as a whole.
pages.title: Structured Academic Controversy

pages.description: A reusable policy in which learners comment on one another's drafts against explicit criteria and each author then revises before the work is judged; expected to improve the revised work, and possibly the reviewers' own later work, where reviewers are calibrated on the criteria, comments point to the draft and suggest changes, revision is required and stakes are formative; no claim tests the full cycle, though peer feedback on writing and peer assessment are each tested against no feedback.
pages.title: Structured Peer Review

pages.description: A unit-level readiness-assurance policy (individual closed-book test, team retest with immediate feedback, appeals, targeted clarification, then team application) whose test-and-feedback steps rest on retrieval evidence and whose team formation, application exercises and peer evaluation do not.
pages.title: Team Based Learning

pages.description: A reusable think, pair, share policy for open questions, in which protected individual think time and a partner exchange of reasoning are expected to widen and improve public responses, conditional on the prompt, pair dynamics, individual accountability and an immediate horizon.
pages.title: Think-Pair-Share

pages.description: A lecture-centered course (lecture, assigned study, then discussion or assessment) is expected to serve information objectives about as well as other methods but to underperform discussion and active-learning courses for thought, attitude and skill objectives and on exams and pass rates; claims test lecture only as a comparator, and the segmented sequence here is untested.
pages.title: Traditional Lecture-Based Instruction

pages.description: A reusable example-first policy for a structured task, qualified by task-specific knowledge, representation and intended outcome.
pages.title: Worked Examples

pages.description: A reusable lesson and unit structure (a short mini-lesson teaching one strategy, a protected block of learners' own work while the teacher confers, then a share) expected to build skill in a practice when the mini-lesson teaches strategies explicitly and support is matched and faded; no claim in this wiki tests the workshop model as a whole, and the nearest, on process writing, found a modest gain that did not reach struggling writers.
pages.title: Workshop Model

pages.description: For a learner whose failure on a content task may be linguistic rather than conceptual, removing avoidable wording barriers while explicitly teaching the few essential terms is expected to improve comprehension of the taught material, with weak evidence for transfer to authentic texts or delayed retention.
pages.title: Accessible Vocabulary & Syntax

pages.description: For learners whose relevant prior knowledge is accurate and is then used by the instruction that follows, an activity that makes it visible before instruction may improve comprehension or retention, while activating topic knowledge alone has often shown little effect and activated misconceptions need confronting.
pages.title: Activation

pages.description: For learners meeting new material in a course, class time spent generating, explaining or applying the content with feedback, rather than only listening, is expected to raise course-end exam and concept-inventory scores, qualified by guidance for novices, the kind of engagement and what else changed with the format.
pages.title: Active Learning

pages.description: When learners on a cumulative, decomposable task start from different observed responses, choosing each next task, hint or check from the learner's own recent responses (rather than one fixed path) may improve aligned achievement, conditional on how well the responses diagnose the learner, what the adaptation changes, and whether support is withdrawn as performance grows.
pages.title: Adaptive Learning

pages.description: For anyone writing or reading an evaluation of an instructional intervention, reporting a standardized effect size with its interval, comparison and measure beside every p value, and reading it against effects for the same kind of outcome rather than a universal label, is expected to lead to better adopt-or-revise decisions than significance alone; no claim in the wiki tests that expectation, though claims show significance and size diverging, significance filtering inflating sizes, and sizes depending on the measure.
pages.title: Always report and interpret effect sizes alongside p values for primary outcomes

pages.description: Comparing a new situation with a provided analogous case, prompted to find the shared relation and followed by the principle, is expected to help learners who do not yet see that structure transfer it to a near new case at a short horizon; analogies from a familiar source domain, far transfer and delayed effects are untested here.
pages.title: Analogical Reasoning

pages.description: For readers of a demanding text, marking it may improve later performance on what was marked, while gains in comprehension are expected only from annotations that make the reader select, explain or question, and remain largely untested.
pages.title: Annotating

pages.description: For a novice or intermediate learner who brings a specific question or attempt to someone with more domain expertise, a consultation in which the expert has the learner explain first, responds with the least help that works, and does less across a series, followed by applying the advice, is expected to improve unaided performance on that task, though no claim here tests expert access as such.
pages.title: Ask Experts

pages.description: Assessment evidence gathered during instruction is expected to support learning when teacher and learner read it against shared criteria, under stakes that let partial understanding show, with a revision step before the outcome is judged.
pages.title: Assessment for Learning

pages.description: For writing and project work, addressing a genuine reader beyond the teacher-as-grader is associated with higher-rated products in small comparisons, conditional on the audience being credible, the criteria explicit and support for revision present.
pages.title: Authentic Audiences & Purposes

pages.description: For a learner whose engagement is controlled by pressure or reward, meaningful choice within structure, a rationale for required work and non-controlling language are expected to sustain motivation and voluntary engagement; their effect on learning outcomes is small, inconsistent and depends on what the learner controls and when.
pages.title: Autonomy

pages.description: For a learner forming an interpretation of another person or group, structured perspective-taking with concrete accounts and comparison of interpretations may improve attitudes towards that group, a relationship qualified by outcome, dose, target and horizon.
pages.title: Building Empathy

pages.description: For school-age learners, a schoolwide plan kept for two or more years (one definition shared by all adults, supervised and organised unstructured times, rehearsed bystander and defender moves, several reporting routes including anonymous ones, and an incident response that protects the target, with separate steps for cyberbullying) is expected to reduce bullying and fear of it more than a response aimed only at the bully and target after incidents; trials of schoolwide behaviour, recess and restorative programmes test schoolwide action against comparison schools, but no claim tests the role-focused design or a cyberbullying response.
pages.title: Bullying Prevention and Intervention

pages.description: For school-age and university learners, making ethical understanding, caring response and moral action part of everyday school life (shared conflict-resolution routines, class meetings, service tied to reflection, moral problems in specific situations across subjects) is expected to change behaviour and civic commitment more than a separate civic or moral course or rule recitation; WWC reviews test three branded programmes against usual practice, finding behaviour effects more often than attitude or achievement effects, but no claim tests the integrated form against a separate course.
pages.title: Character Education

pages.description: A brief, recurring prompt for learners to report their state can guide the next instructional move, but only when the report is read as uncertain evidence, checked against performance where accuracy matters, and acted on.
pages.title: Check-ins

pages.description: For a learner who cannot yet treat a task's elements as familiar units, presenting the material in meaningful units with boundaries at conceptual breaks, then recombining them, is expected to ease processing and may improve immediate performance; what counts as a unit depends on that learner's prior knowledge.
pages.title: Chunking

pages.description: For a group sharing a classroom, a room arranged for visibility with moderate displays, taught procedures kept separate from a few positively stated rules, tasks pitched at moderate difficulty with structure that fades, and prepared transitions are expected to reduce disruption and lost time compared with improvising them; no claim tests these moves directly, and the nearest test is a meta-analysis of universal classroom management programmes against usual practice.
pages.title: Classroom Space and Procedural Design

pages.description: For learners without an organization of their own for unfamiliar material, making its organization explicit (signals, lean organizers, graphics that match the content and task) may improve what they select and recall on immediate tests, an effect qualified by prior knowledge, structural match and outcome.
pages.title: Clear Structure

pages.description: For learners working toward a concept or principle, tasks that require them to explain, compare, predict or justify beyond what was presented, with enough guidance to produce something correct, are expected to improve immediate understanding and near transfer more than tasks completed by recall or copying, with weak evidence for classroom and delayed outcomes and no claim testing cognitive activation as a dimension of teaching quality.
pages.title: Cognitive Activation

pages.description: For a learner who holds a confident but inaccurate explanation, meeting evidence it cannot account for and then being helped to resolve the mismatch is expected to improve conceptual understanding more than the correct account alone, with weak evidence that the revision lasts or that conflict without support helps.
pages.title: Cognitive Disequilibrium

pages.description: Revisiting the same concepts across several cases, perspectives or representations that differ in how the concept applies, with explicit prompts to compare them, is expected to help learners with some but rigid knowledge of an ill-structured domain transfer it to a new case at a short horizon; it may cost factual recall, novices may need a simpler start, and delayed effects are untested here.
pages.title: Cognitive Flexibility

pages.description: Across a sequence, matching how presentation, task order and support distribute processing demand to a learner's current task-specific capacity is expected to improve learning, while keeping effortful processing that the intended outcome and horizon need; in the wiki, single levers and two whole load-reducing designs are tested, the withdraw-and-restore policy is not.
pages.title: Cognitive Load Management

pages.description: For a task-specific novice on high-element-interactivity material, reducing avoidable processing is expected to improve performance or efficiency, a relationship that weakens or reverses as task-specific expertise grows.
pages.title: Cognitive Load Theory

pages.description: For a learner whose attempts stall in a way that looks like a habit of approach (holistic or analytic, quick or deliberate), teaching the approach the task requires to everyone who needs it, faded across sessions, is expected to help more than matching tasks or formats to a measured style; no claim in the wiki tests either use of cognitive styles, and the matching evidence, from learning styles, runs against it.
pages.title: Cognitive Styles

pages.description: When learners study an explanation of something they do not yet understand, leaving out interesting but irrelevant words, pictures, sounds and music (seductive details) is expected to improve comprehension and transfer over the same explanation with them added; the wiki's claims test this, in a meta-analysis and many experiments, and record effects that range from large in one research programme to small or absent elsewhere, depending on the material, its pacing and complexity, and the learner's prior knowledge, working memory and attentional control.
pages.title: Coherence Principle

pages.description: For learners who can take part in the task, working jointly so that each member must engage with the others' reasoning is expected to raise individually measured understanding over working alone on the same task, for goals that gain from explaining and reconciling ideas; co-presence, equal participation or group satisfaction alone are not expected to show it.
pages.title: Collaborative Learning

pages.description: For an adult, often older, learner whose hearing or eyesight has declined, presenting each new item both spoken and written or shown, in a well-lit room with little outside noise and with control of pace, is expected to let them take in more of the new material than speech alone; no claim in the wiki tests this with such learners, only spoken-plus-written words, captions and pacing with other learners.
pages.title: Compensate for age-related sensory impairments by combining audio input with visual presentation

pages.description: For second-language learners building general vocabulary, deliberate study of selected words combined with reading and listening for meaning (glossed, with recurring words) is expected to give more words and better retention than either mode alone, with the deliberate share largest while text coverage is below about 95%; two thin claims test the combination, none tests its order, ratio or dose.
pages.title: Combine intentional and incidental vocabulary learning rather than relying on incidental learning alone

pages.description: For adults and professionals entering a shared practice, sustained and structured participation with more experienced members, under norms of trust and critical inquiry, is proposed to change their practice and understanding over a term or more, though the wiki holds only descriptive, qualitative and argued evidence for it.
pages.title: Communities of Practice

pages.description: For a learner whose coursework stays school-internal, giving the work a real role in a community is associated with civic attitudes, self-reported growth and deeper reflection when the work is tied to course concepts, reflection is structured and relationships are supported; no claim here tests its effect on content learning.
pages.title: Community-Based Learning

pages.description: For learners in a discussion-based course whose shared inquiry stalls at sharing ideas, the CoI framework proposes that designed social, cognitive and teaching presence together move discourse towards resolution, but the wiki holds only survey associations and descriptive profiles of the presences, no test of that effect on learning.
pages.title: Community of Inquiry

pages.description: Scoring a learner's response on a task that represents the intended capability against explicit criteria and a stated threshold, by consistent assessors, is expected to support better teaching, progression and certification decisions than a rank or seat time, though no claim here tests that comparison and assessor agreement is not guaranteed.
pages.title: Competency-Based Assessment

pages.description: When learners must come to understand an abstract symbol system or formal structure (an equation, a group property, a permutation formula), starting with a concrete model of it, moving through an iconic picture of the same model, and ending with the abstract notation, each step explicitly linked to the last, is expected to produce better learning and transfer than starting abstract or staying concrete; one experiment, reported second-hand, tests the full sequence here, a meta-analysis supports concrete materials over symbols alone, and the rest is a review's argument and one teaching experiment.
pages.title: Concreteness Fading

pages.description: For a learner who has committed to a judgment where the evidence could point either way, a prompt to generate specific reasons the opposite could be right, then to decide again, is expected to reduce confirmation, anchoring and overconfidence biases more than a general warning to be objective; no claim in this wiki tests it directly, and the one claim on it rests on a review that names the method without testing it.
pages.title: Considering The Opposite

pages.description: When words and a picture explain one thing and neither makes sense without the other, placing each word next to the part of the picture it describes, and presenting narration at the same time as the animation it describes, is expected to improve learning over separated or successive presentation for learners new to the material; meta-analyses test this (spatial and temporal effects of similar size), with larger effects for complex material and system-paced media and a reversal reported for experienced learners.
pages.title: Contiguity Principle (Spatial and Temporal)

pages.description: For learners who can take part in the task, structured small-group work in which each member's learning is individually checked and counts toward the group's success is expected to raise individually measured achievement over several weeks, more than individualistic or competitive work; grouping alone is not expected to.
pages.title: Cooperative Learning

pages.description: A decision about a learner is expected to be more accurate when the score matches the question asked: a criterion-referenced report against skills defined in advance for what a learner can do and should be taught next, a norm-referenced score read against a fitting norm group (and never alone) for relative standing and selection, and a diagnostic profile for why a learner struggles; no claim here tests the relationship.
pages.title: Criterion- and Norm-Referenced Testing

pages.description: For learners whose instruction draws on contexts they do not recognise or see no stake in, building some tasks, examples and assessments from their own cultural, community, family and work experience, tied to the concept taught, is expected to raise engagement, open sharing of developing thinking and the competence an assessment can see; no claim here compares it with the same content taught without that connection.
pages.title: Cultural & Life Experiences Connections

pages.description: For learners whose home or community norms of talk, questioning, competition, time and conduct differ from the classroom's, widening the classroom's norms (longer wait time, private or all-student response, cooperative options, conventions taught explicitly) and reading a departure from a norm as a possible difference of convention before judging ability or defiance is expected to make questioning show more of what learners know and to raise participation and reduce disciplinary exclusion; no claim here tests this, though claims test wait time, cooperative structures and empathic discipline in general populations.
pages.title: Culturally Responsive Classroom Norms

pages.description: For learners who have just shared an experience (a simulation, case, team exercise or real event), a facilitated debrief that establishes what happened, asks for their reasoning at a few decision points against stated criteria, gives task- and process-level feedback and ends with one change to try is expected to improve the next comparable performance more than the experience alone or an unstructured recap, though no claim here compares an experience with and without a debrief.
pages.title: Debriefing

pages.description: For a learner who can already perform a task but has stopped improving on part of it, repeated attempts on that one diagnosed component, set just beyond reliable performance, judged against an explicit standard with feedback and a deliberate change on each next attempt, are expected to improve whole-task performance more than repeating the whole task; no claim tests this in schooling, and the nearest causal evidence is simulation training with deliberate practice in the health professions.
pages.title: Deliberate Practice

pages.description: A recurring cycle in which an educator gathers outside evidence about their own practice, names the assumption it shows and changes one decision is expected to make their reading of learners more accurate and less excluding; no claim tests this whole, and one brief empathic-discipline exercise tests a narrow version.
pages.title: Developing Your Cultural Awareness

pages.description: Putting part of a course on a digital tool is expected to help only through the method it makes affordable (more practice with feedback, adaptive hints, prompts to explain, visible progress) and not through the medium itself; no claim here tests a digital against a non-digital version of the same method.
pages.title: Digital Learning

pages.description: For a learner with no working method for a structured target, explicit explanation, modelling and guided practice with checks is expected to beat minimally guided discovery on near-term performance, qualified by task-specific expertise, age, outcome type and horizon.
pages.title: Direct Instruction

pages.description: For adolescents who read adequately in general but meet a discipline's texts as novices, a semester or more of instruction that names, models and has them practise the discipline's own reading and reasoning moves on its own texts is expected to improve comprehension of new texts in that discipline and the practised kind of disciplinary thinking; two studies test this against usual or textbook instruction, none against generic strategy instruction, and the one writing measure showed no gain.
pages.title: Disciplinary Literacy

pages.description: For learners studying a topic in which race shapes outcomes or experience, naming race explicitly around a shared text, case or data set, under agreed norms with optional disclosure and a closing debrief, is expected to yield more specific, better-evidenced analysis than neutral treatment or unstructured talk without raising risk for learners in the minority; no claim in the wiki tests this.
pages.title: Discussing Race

pages.description: For a task too large for one learner to hold or do alone, putting part of the work into shared representations, tools or partners is expected to raise performance with those aids present, and to build what the learner can do alone only when the parts the target requires stay with the learner and the learner's decisions to rely on aids are calibrated; no claim recorded in the wiki tests distributed against individual work at first hand, while single studies test how much to hand to an AI tool, feedback that calibrates offloading, and the form of a group's shared representation.
pages.title: Distributed Cognition

pages.description: For a learner without a working model of a structure or process, pairing the words that explain it with a visual of the same idea, supplied or learner-made, is expected to improve comprehension over words alone; claims test each half against words alone, none tests the sequence, direct tests favour provided over learner-built organizers for transfer, and the drawing supports tested did not help.
pages.title: Dual Coding

pages.description: For learners starting a new stage, course or unit whose tasks assume earlier capabilities, checking each learner's starting response on those capabilities and adjusting the entry point, support and setting to it is expected to let more of them reach the stage's goals than holding them back until judged ready or teaching all from one assumed starting point; no claim in the wiki tests this directly, though claims on delayed entry, repetition and preschool attendance bear on it.
pages.title: Educational Readiness

pages.description: For a group of learners in a shared space, a classroom-wide plan put in place before problems arise and kept consistently (relationships, taught rules and routines, unobtrusive redirection, a short consistent response to persistent misbehavior, self-control taught with external controls planned to fade, and corrections checked for cultural meaning) is expected to reduce disruption and raise engaged time more than improvised practice; one meta-analysis tests planned universal management against usual practice and a K–5 practice guide rates taught behavior expectations as strongly supported, but no claim tests the six-part plan or any of its traditions.
pages.title: Effective Classroom Management Plan Criteria

pages.description: For a learner with relevant prior knowledge studying facts or prose, answering why-questions about each statement or generating their own connections is expected to improve recall and recognition over reading it, at a cost in time; randomised experiments with school students test this for science facts, and one experiment finds the reverse for novice undergraduates learning a probability calculation.
pages.title: Elaborative Reasoning

pages.description: For a learner whose participation in a task is low, a personal contact, a visible reason for the task and visible, reachable progress are expected to raise observed on-task time, completion and persistence, and that engagement is expected to raise learning only when the task requires thinking with the target; claims test single conditions on single outcomes, and none tests engagement as a whole or shows that it causes learning.
pages.title: Engagement

pages.description: When learners must judge claims, explicit teaching and practice of the standards for a particular kind of evidence (checking who is behind a web source, judging a study's methods, justifying an argument with evidence) is associated with better judgments of that kind, measured up to five weeks later; the gains have not been shown to carry over to other kinds of evidence.
pages.title: Epistemic Cognition

pages.description: For a learner who can already follow a correct solution, comparing an incorrect solution with a correct one, explaining the error and seeing the correction is expected to improve conceptual understanding, and correcting errors (confident ones first) to improve later recall, but the evidence is a few short studies, mostly children in mathematics and adults on recall items.
pages.title: Error Analysis

pages.description: For adolescent and adult novices who judge unfamiliar web sources by their own features, several lessons teaching and practising a move off the page (searching what independent sources say about who is behind it) are expected to improve credibility judgments of new sites up to five weeks later; one claim tests this package against untaught classes, though not against a checklist taught over the same number of sessions, nor for research articles or primary documents.
pages.title: Evaluating Sources

pages.description: For a teacher, designer or purchaser choosing an approach for other people's learners, writing the belief as a claim some result could refute, seeking a comparison that could have come out otherwise and the case against it, and adopting as a recorded local trial where no comparison exists, is expected to select approaches that do more for learners than choosing by impression, popularity or philosophy; no claim in the wiki tests this for practitioners' own decisions, and one school-reform evaluation tests a school-level version with mixed results.
pages.title: Evidence-Based Teaching and Scientific Reasoning

pages.description: For adults in transition who can name few people to ask about their goal, repeated structured contact with the same peers, outreach by staff or mentors, and brokered introductions with a follow-up step are expected to yield usable new ties, less isolation and, more slowly, persistence and access to opportunity, though no claim in the wiki tests this against leaving networking to the learner.
pages.title: Expanding Social Networks

pages.description: For learners building applied, professional or interpersonal capability, an experience followed by structured reflection and a further attempt with feedback is expected to improve performance and transfer, while unguided experience for novices learns less than guided instruction.
pages.title: Experiential Learning

pages.description: For adult novices with a device, especially older or low-confidence adults, demonstrating one short routine at a time on their own device, having them do it at once with help that responds to each attempt, and withdrawing that help as they succeed is expected to produce more accurate unaided use of those routines than exploration or explanation alone, though no claim in the wiki tests this for computer basics.
pages.title: Explicit Instruction: Computer Basics

pages.description: For a novice searcher who types whole questions and stops at the first results, explicit modelling of a routine for turning a question into terms, building and revising queries and checking results, practised on real inquiry questions with feedback on the queries, is expected to find more relevant sources with less abandonment than unguided exploration, though no claim in the wiki tests search instruction directly.
pages.title: Explicit Instruction: Internet Search

pages.description: For a learner who can compute but not yet choose a method for word or non-routine problems, explicitly modelling when and why a strategy fits, comparing methods side by side and guiding justified choice are expected to build flexible, accurate problem solving, though no claim in the wiki tests strategy instruction against its absence.
pages.title: Explicit Instruction: Math Strategies

pages.description: For a learner who reads print adequately but navigates linked online texts without a goal, explicit modelled instruction in a few online reading moves (goal and questions before opening links, choosing links against the goal, a running record of pages, returning from drift, combining pages), practised on curated then open sets of pages with prompts that fade, is expected to improve comprehension and integration across pages; no claim tests this, and the nearest evidence is print strategy instruction and computer-based metacognitive prompts.
pages.title: Explicit Instruction: Online Reading Strategies

pages.description: For a learner whose comprehension or use of language is limited by particular unknown words, explicitly teaching a small selected set and then arranging repeated encounters and use across contexts is expected to improve knowledge of those words and comprehension of texts that use them more than exposure alone, which claims test for school-age and second-language learners, but not for general comprehension, dose or schedule.
pages.title: Explicit Instruction: Vocabulary

pages.description: For learners exploring how a system behaves, a computer tool that returns the result of each idea in seconds is expected to let them test more hypotheses with less frustration and spend the saved time interpreting, improving conceptual understanding and inquiry skill when the exploration is guided; no claim in the wiki tests the speed of the cycle itself, though guidance during inquiry is supported.
pages.title: Use computer tools that let students explore hypotheses and solutions faster so they can test many ideas without frustration

pages.description: For a learner whose performance can be observed, information about it is expected to improve later performance only when the loop closes (the information says what to change, a next attempt uses it, and that attempt is checked again on a new item); corrective feedback and correct-and-recheck programmes are supported on average, but no claim here tests a closed loop against the same feedback without a next attempt.
pages.title: Feedback Loops

pages.description: For a second-language learner, treating errors according to the activity's objective (accuracy or meaning), the learner's competence with the form, their affect and whether earlier corrections have taken hold is expected to improve accuracy at immediate and delayed tests better than one uniform correction policy; no claim in the wiki tests that matching, though corrective feedback as a whole has a durable effect and correction forms differ.
pages.title: Employ flexible error treatment strategies matched to objectives, competence, affect, and correction effectiveness

pages.description: In a class whose learners differ on the current task, forming temporary similar-need and mixed groups for a stated purpose from recent task evidence, and re-forming them as the evidence changes, is expected to match support and challenge to need better than one whole-class format, and to keep what targeted support gains without the costs fixed attainment sorting shows on grades, pass rates and the lowest group's classroom climate; no claim here tests flexible grouping itself, and the fixed-sorting evidence (one district's algebra policy) shows test-score gains for high attainers as well as those costs.
pages.title: Flexible Grouping

pages.description: For learners who can follow a topic's first explanation on their own, moving that first exposure before the live session and spending the freed time on application with feedback is expected to give better course outcomes than spending live time on the same exposition, provided learners prepare and the home time is not simply added; one meta-analysis of undergraduate health-professions courses found flipped classes ahead of lecture-based ones on exam performance (SMD 0.57), at low certainty with very high heterogeneity, and no claim here tests it with home time held equal.
pages.title: Flipped Learning

pages.description: A conditional model relating learner state, activity and subsequent observation; the linked pattern specifies a reusable design policy.
pages.title: Formative Assessment

pages.description: For learners producing ideas or products in a domain they partly know, open prompts with many answers, generating kept apart in time from judging, grading and reward, and own ideas before AI are expected to yield more varied ideas, sustained interest and better unaided generation later; no claim in the wiki tests the relationship as a whole, though neighbouring claims test rewards, praise, AI sequencing, explicit strategy instruction and a pause before choosing.
pages.title: Fostering Creative Thinking

pages.description: In settings where learners choose whether, what and how long to engage, several entry points, a start from their own interests, no grades or expected rewards for taking part, and an activity that responds to each attempt are expected to lengthen voluntary engagement and, with feedback on the target idea, to improve understanding; no claim tests a free-choice environment as a whole, and one randomised exhibit study tests the feedback part.
pages.title: Free-Choice Learning Environment Design

pages.description: For a learner whose disruptive behavior recurs despite sound classroom management, identifying what triggers it and what it gets them, then changing the trigger and teaching a replacement that meets the same need, with consistent documented responses, is expected to reduce it more than generic or escalating discipline, though no claim here tests a function-based plan against a generic one.
pages.title: Functional Behavior Assessment

pages.description: For a learner who has not yet reached a stated capability, a game whose winning move is the target reasoning, played over several sessions inside a course of instruction, with modelling for novices and a debrief that asks for the reasoning outside the game, is expected to improve aligned outside-game performance over passive or no instruction; meta-analyses find small-to-moderate average gains that vary widely and disappear against active non-game instruction, and enjoyment and game score are separate outcomes.
pages.title: Game-based Learning

pages.description: For learners whose bottleneck is keeping going through repeated practice, a game layer (points, levels, badges, team scores, a theme) added to sound instruction is expected to give a small gain in later performance when it rewards accuracy and improvement rather than activity, leaves meaningful choice and keeps decoration tied to content; one meta-analysis tests gamification on average, and no claim tests these conditions.
pages.title: Gamification

pages.description: When a learner holds a specific, challenging goal for a task, with a plan for reaching it and feedback to check progress against it, effort and task performance may rise, qualified by task complexity and the learner's expertise (process goals before outcome goals for novices), commitment and self-efficacy, and whether the outcome measured is behaviour, regulation or learning.
pages.title: Goal Setting & Monitoring

pages.description: For learners who do not yet hold a material's structure, a diagram whose layout matches that structure, provided first and later built and explained by the learner, is expected to improve comprehension and retention over text alone; concept-map meta-analyses test this for node-link maps, and no claim tests other organizer forms, partial organizers or fading.
pages.title: Graphic Organizers

pages.description: For a learner who has seen a model but cannot yet perform a structured task alone, several practice attempts with support and feedback still available, reduced as unaided success appears, are expected to produce more accurate independent performance than no practice or unsupported practice, though no claim here tests guided against independent practice directly.
pages.title: Guided Practice

pages.description: For a reader who cannot yet tell what matters in a dense or unfamiliar text or task, a supplied guide that marks the essential points, shows the structure, glosses unknown terms and asks the reader to use it is expected to improve comprehension and recall over the same material without it; claims test its components (cues, guided notes, organizers, pictures, glosses), and none tests a whole handout or reading guide as such.
pages.title: Handouts/Online Guides/Visual Reading Aids

pages.description: When a target has components that competing methods serve unequally (content knowledge and application, language form and use, precise and expressive language), giving each component to the method its evidence favours and checking each separately is expected to cover more of the target than adopting either method wholesale; no claim tests this as a general rule, though one trial shows two methods each winning on a different outcome and vocabulary syntheses report combined instruction ahead of either alone.
pages.title: Harmonize opposites: strike a balance between competing educational ideas rather than embracing one method wholesale

pages.description: For a learner acquiring a school or majority language, continuing to use and develop the heritage language is expected not to slow that acquisition and, at an academic level, to transfer to it; the support is associational and second-hand, and the one randomised programme-level test in the wiki found no significant difference for English learners.
pages.title: Preserve Heritage Language While Acquiring an Additional Language

pages.description: For a learner without an organisation of their own for interconnected content, giving a usable whole early (a map of the main ideas, a model or a complete simple task) and keeping later details attached to it is expected to help integrative tasks more than learning details in isolation, unless the whole is too complex for a novice to follow; no claim tests whole-first against parts-first, and one small set of physics experiments on hierarchical organisation bears on it.
pages.title: Holistic Learning

pages.description: For adult learners, a course in which the educator hears and answers views unlike their own, brings social events in as material to question and leaves action to the learner is expected to strengthen learners' sense of voice, systemic accounts of social problems and readiness to act, but no claim in the wiki tests this, and the one controlled survey found more frequent discussion did not predict more critical reflection.
pages.title: Adopt humanistic and radical approaches so adult learners develop as individuals and can question social injustice

pages.description: For a learner practising a task where errors can be seen, correction before the next attempt is expected to stop errors being rehearsed, but whether the timing matters, immediate rather than delayed feedback improving delayed retention, is not settled: the comparisons recorded here find no advantage or favour delay.
pages.title: Immediate Feedback

pages.description: For adolescents and young adults in a self-regulation programme, adding coached support for the adults around them (their own regulation, and rehearsed co-regulation of the young person) is expected to make gains larger and more transferable, a practice brief's guideline that no claim in this wiki tests directly; neighbouring syntheses show coached parent training beating information alone for younger children.
pages.title: Include parents, teachers, or mentors in any self-regulation intervention and support their own skills and coaching capacity

pages.description: For school science learners, inquiry that is guided (prompts, feedback, teacher-led explanation and a synthesis) is associated with better conceptual understanding than comparison instruction, while unguided discovery of essential content learns less than explicit instruction for novices.
pages.title: Inquiry-based Learning

pages.description: For a learner who gets stuck on course work between contacts, published channels, a kept reply window, an invitation that makes asking normal and replies that respond to the learner's attempt are expected to raise the share who get help before they disengage, though no claim here tests instructor accessibility as such.
pages.title: Instructor Accessibility

pages.description: When the goal is to tell apart categories or problem types that resemble one another, mixing examples or problems of different kinds in practice (interleaving) is expected to improve later classification and problem choice over practising one kind at a time (blocking); a meta-analysis of 59 studies supports this for visual categories and, more weakly, mathematics, finds no benefit for expository texts and a reversal for word lists, and finds the benefit grows with how similar the categories are.
pages.title: Interleaving

pages.description: For a learner keeping a journal over a course, short recurring entries written to task-specific, metacognitive prompts and then read and used are expected to improve understanding and self-regulation more than an unprompted or unused diary, though no claim tests keeping a journal against not keeping one on a learning outcome, and a diary alone showed no detected gain.
pages.title: Journaling

pages.description: For a learner who holds a topic as unconnected facts and must later use it for tasks that cut across it, teaching the content with an explicit organization built for those tasks, and having learners sort into, explain and rebuild that organization from memory, is expected to improve integrative tasks but not single-detail tasks; one small 1979 physics report tests the core contrast, and no claim tests other kinds of organization or a course-long framework.
pages.title: Knowledge Organization

pages.description: For a learner working through second-language video or text a little above their level, keeping the material whole and putting helps (glossary, replay, first-language explanation, model answer after an attempt, hints before answers) one step away under the learner's control is expected to support comprehension and vocabulary at least as well as withholding or pushing the same helps; no claim here tests on-demand against pushed helps, and learner control in general averages near zero.
pages.title: Keep the learner in control of the information flow with on-demand tools and supports

pages.description: For a student with a disability, bringing supports into the general class and school life and moving the student to a separate setting only for a documented need the supported class cannot meet, decided case by case by a team and reviewed against data, is expected to give learning no worse than separate placement and fuller participation; one review of non-randomised studies finds no average difference between inclusive and segregated placement, and no claim tests the case-by-case decision itself.
pages.title: Least Restrictive Environment

pages.description: For learners who enter a program to get work soon, tying each program element to a named job entry point (an early employer-recognized credential, training timed to hiring or apprenticeship intake, employer contact, visible wage steps) is expected to raise entry into that work, but no claim tests the linking against the same program untied; apprenticeship-versus-other-route evaluations and program reports are the nearest evidence.
pages.title: Link program elements to workforce entry points and employer-recognized credentials so learners see an immediate economic payoff

pages.description: When a learner's response on a unit check falls short of a stated criterion, corrective support and a further check before advancing may raise later unit and course performance, qualified by the validity of the check, the quality of the correction, the time it costs and the horizon assessed.
pages.title: Mastery Learning

pages.description: For adults adopting an innovation in their work, support whose form and content are matched to each person's assessed Stages of Concern and Levels of Use, and kept up after use begins, is expected to move concerns and use forward more than uniform support, though no claim in this wiki tests matched against unmatched support.
pages.title: Match the form and content of staff development interventions to clients' assessed Stages of Concern

pages.description: For a learner who can perform something at the end of a session, planning later encounters that make them reactivate and use the material, and judging security only on a delayed unaided check, is expected to leave more available at the horizon than treating one fluent exposure as finished; no claim tests this as a whole, only its spacing and retrieval routes and a post-learning exercise-timing effect.
pages.title: Memory Consolidation

pages.description: A learner doing real work in a role or programme new to them, paired over time with a more experienced person who observes that work, responds with modelling and specific feedback, meets regularly, stays out of judging them and hands judgement over, is expected to improve observed practice and persistence; the strongest test in the wiki is a meta-analysis of causal teacher-coaching studies (practice 0.49 SD, students' test scores 0.18 SD, effects shrinking at scale), one randomised student-coaching evaluation found higher persistence but not completion, and one randomised induction study found no first-year gains.
pages.title: Mentoring and Coaching

pages.description: For a learner unsettled at the start of demanding work, a short optional attention routine tied to the next task is expected to support settling and self-regulation, and only through that the task itself; no claim here tests a classroom routine, and the one tutor experiment that added mindfulness found no gain in learning or anxiety.
pages.title: Mindfulness Activities

pages.description: For a learner new to a precise response or a set of new pairings, keeping responses almost always correct (a tolerance narrowed in small steps, mediators linked to known items, cues faded across trials, every error corrected at once) is expected to give accurate unaided performance with fewer rehearsed errors than errorful trial and error, though no claim in the wiki tests this with human learners and cue support kept high can weaken retention.
pages.title: Teach response precision and new associations with minimal errors, using mediators and stimulus fading

pages.description: For student writers receiving comments on their work, comments written as complete, specific sentences, legible, limited to a few priorities and following a routine explained in advance are expected to be understood and acted on with less frustration than cryptic, illegible or exhaustive commentary; no claim in the wiki tests this directly, and the nearest evidence is learners' ratings of clearer feedback and reports that some students are overwhelmed by automated feedback.
pages.title: Minimize student frustration by making feedback clear, legible, focused, and transparent

pages.description: For a learner who must recall arbitrary items (terms, foreign words, lists, ordered steps), teaching a specific mnemonic with its meaning made explicit, then practising recall from the cue and without it, is expected to improve recall of those items but not understanding or transfer; claims test this for students with mild disabilities, and for learners in general rate mnemonics below retrieval and spaced practice.
pages.title: Mnemonic Device

pages.description: When words explain a picture or animation that learners must look at as they hear or read them, presenting the words as speech rather than printed text is expected to improve learning, most of all in system-paced, complex lessons for novices; claims test this (two meta-analyses and a review of 17 experiments), and they report it vanishing when learners set the pace, in social-science content, and as learners gain expertise.
pages.title: Modality Principle

pages.description: For a novice on a task whose key decisions a finished product hides, a model that narrates those decisions, studied actively and followed at once by supported practice, is expected to give better unaided performance than the product alone or no model, though no claim here tests live or narrated modelling directly; the evidence is carried from worked examples and self-explanation.
pages.title: Modeling

pages.description: For a learner whose effort or persistence is low, motivation is expected to rise when the design repairs the component that is low for that learner (expectancy of success, task value, ownership, or belonging) rather than adding generic boosts, and to raise learning only through effort on a task that demands thinking; claims test single components, and none tests the matching relationship.
pages.title: Motivation

pages.description: For a learner without a working model of a structure or process, a relevant picture placed with the words that explain it may improve a learning test over words alone, qualified by redundancy, decorative additions, pacing, prior knowledge and assessment horizon.
pages.title: Multimedia Learning
